solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Very nimble, moving freely

parts.note: V is the standard abbreviation for very
nimble and agile are synonyms

explanation.surface: Someone light on their feet is praised for being quick and unconstrained.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one long description, but the first two words are the wordplay and the last two the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A biological term for organisms able to move about freely, as opposed to sessile ones fixed in place.

clue.text: Various later parts dismissed by Val Kilmer's agent

indicators.note: the closing portions of more than one word are sent away, so each word keeps only its opening

parts.note: the first name with its final letter dropped
the surname with its last three letters dropped

explanation.surface: An actor's representative has been trimming the actor's later roles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' sounds like film roles, but it means the ends of the two names. Val Kilmer is the American film actor.
explanation.definitionFit: In India a vakil is an attorney or authorised representative acting on someone's behalf, hence an agent.

clue.text: Celebrity in funny exposé eviscerated Turkish sailor

indicators.note: one thing sitting inside another means one string of letters goes within the other

parts.note: a gag is a joke, something funny
a lion is a celebrated person, as in a literary lion

indicators.note: to eviscerate is to gut, removing the insides and leaving only the outer shell

parts.note: only the first and last letters of the word are kept

explanation.surface: A famous person is caught up in a comic revelation that savages a Turkish seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny' looks like an adjective for the exposé but is a noun source; 'Celebrity' is a lion, an old term for a social star.
explanation.definitionFit: Galiongee is an old term for a seaman in the Turkish navy, from the Turkish word for a galleon crewman.

clue.text: Retired sleuth discarded lead necessary to supply a motive

indicators.note: letters needed by a phrase are part of it, so they sit within those words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A detective out of service drops a clue needed to provide a reason for a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about detective work, but sleuth here is the old word for a sleuth-hound, a bloodhound, and lead is its leash.
explanation.definitionFit: An obsolete word for the leash of a hunting hound; retired and discarded both flag that it is no longer in use.

clue.text: Throbbing form of flu is interrupting film

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one part goes inside the other

parts.note: a pic is a picture, a film

indicators.note: a new form of something is a reshaping, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pounding version of influenza breaks into a cinema screening.
explanation.walkthrough: A throbbing head suggests illness, so the surface hangs together; the film is just a three-letter word for a picture.
explanation.definitionFit: An old adjective meaning causing or exhibiting the pulse, so beating rhythmically, as a pulse does.

clue.text: Grow straight and erect, for Cowper prizes crownless tree

definitions.text: Grow straight and erect, for Cowper

indicators.note: without a crown means the top is gone, and in a down light the top is the first letter

parts.note: cups are trophies awarded as prizes
a fruit tree

explanation.surface: A poet's tree wins awards while missing its top and growing tall.
explanation.walkthrough: William Cowper was an 18th-century English poet; the word is credited to him, so the definition names its source.
explanation.definitionFit: Cowper used the verb for shooting upward like a spear, so rising tall and straight is its literal meaning.

clue.text: Second officers' hammocks lightly scratch, said dragoons

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
on ships a cot was a framed hammock-bed slung for officers

indicators.note: something said is spoken, so it is the pronunciation that counts, not the spelling

parts.note: to graze skin is to scrape it lightly

explanation.surface: A naval scene where junior officers' sleeping slings get scuffed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is shipboard; 'said' applies only to the last word of the wordplay. The Scots Greys were a famous British cavalry regiment.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Scots Greys were a regiment of dragoons, mounted soldiers, named for their grey horses.

clue.text: Underground passage mostly barred after confusion

indicators.note: most of something but not all means its last letter is dropped
coming after another part means this one is placed second in the answer

parts.note: being in a fog is being confused
barred from a place means kept out

explanation.surface: A tunnel is generally closed off following some mix-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the barred piece second. A fogou is an Iron Age underground passage found in Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cornish name for a prehistoric souterrain, a stone-lined tunnel built below ground for storage or refuge.

clue.text: Part of brass instrument you covered with crook and organ for The Spinners

indicators.note: a thing covered by another is wrapped inside it

parts.note: crim is slang short for criminal
the flared mouth of a trumpet or horn
text-speak spelling of you

explanation.surface: A musical scene: a trumpet part, a shepherd's crook and an organ provided for the 1960s folk group The Spinners.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spinners sound like the Liverpool folk band, but they are spiders; 'crook' is a criminal, not a staff.
explanation.definitionFit: The cribellum is a spinning plate on certain spiders that produces fine woolly silk, so a silk-making body part.

clue.text: Once every so often engaged in little one's heart

parts.note: engaged in work is being at work
Scottish word for small

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle letter is kept

parts.note: the middle letter of the three

explanation.surface: Someone occasionally busies themselves with the core of a small child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' marks an archaic word. The sense is 'between', as in between whiles: intermittently.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic form of between; at intervals, between times, is how something happens occasionally.

clue.text: Ceremonial gift tokens delay salary cuts, all at the centre

indicators.note: each word is reduced to what lies in its middle

parts.note: the two central letters of a six-letter word
the central letter of a five-letter word
the two central letters of a six-letter word
the two central letters of a four-letter word

explanation.surface: An employer's gift vouchers postpone the pay cuts, which hit everybody in head office.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like an office memo; 'tokens' looks as if it belongs with the gift, but it supplies the first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A khilat, or kellaut, is a robe of honour bestowed by an Eastern ruler, a ceremonial present.

clue.text: Dog with little hair is to shed third of skin

parts.note: a snake sloughs, or sheds, its skin

indicators.note: the third item in a word is a single letter counted from its start

parts.note: the third letter

explanation.surface: A short-haired dog moults part of its coat.
explanation.walkthrough: The moulting surface ties neatly to a dog, and 'skin' looks like what is shed, but it only gives one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The sloughi is a smooth-coated North African sighthound, so its coat is short and sparse.

clue.text: Part of bow string along back

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word runs right to left

parts.note: to string someone along is to deceive or fool them

explanation.surface: An archer's bowstring is drawn back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bow' and 'string' suggest archery, but this bow is the front of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The loof is the after part of a ship's bow, where the planking begins to curve, a nautical term.

clue.text: Each Spenserian, superficially into modest conduct of Spenser

indicators.note: going into something puts it inside

parts.note: demure means modest and reserved
EA is the standard abbreviation for each

indicators.note: the surface of a word is its outside, so only the outer letters count

parts.note: first and last letters only

explanation.surface: Every poet in the Spenser school shows a shallow interest in proper behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: The repetition of Spenser hides that the first is just letters; the answer is Spenser's own spelling of demeanour.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund Spenser used this form for demeanour, meaning behaviour or bearing, in The Faerie Queene.

clue.text: More little insects bringing the second one to the top workers on the move

indicators.text: bringing the second one to the top
indicators.note: one letter is moved from its place to the front, a rearrangement of the word

parts.note: smaller
taken as a common example of insects

explanation.surface: Smaller insects carry a comrade up to the head of the colony, a nest of busy workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' means the letter I, so the second I in the comparative moves to the front. Worker ants make the insects seem part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Itinerants are people travelling from place to place for work, such as seasonal labourers and peddlers.

clue.text: He's like a worker around children at agreed exhibits

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
to exhibit is to put on show, so the words display the letters inside them

parts.note: the run from the end of the first word through the start of the third

explanation.surface: A man resembling a labourer shows off around kids at an approved display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' and 'worker' suggest a human employee; the creature is an ant, and worker is the ant caste.
explanation.definitionFit: An ergataner is a male ant resembling a worker ant, lacking wings; 'he' supplies the male.

clue.text: US rifle sighting device packaged with letter's contents

indicators.note: something packaged is wrapped inside other material
the contents of something are its insides, without the edges

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters
a telescopic sight on a gun

explanation.surface: A gunsight is mailed out along with whatever is in an envelope.
explanation.walkthrough: The posted-parcel picture is natural; 'letter' is the source of letters, not correspondence.
explanation.definitionFit: An escopette is a kind of carbine or short rifle formerly used in the American Southwest.

clue.text: Sharply goad inferior, always changing sides

indicators.note: left and right trade places, so each letter for one side is swapped for the other

parts.note: lower in rank or quality

explanation.surface: Someone spurs on a weaker partner, a turncoat who keeps switching allegiance.
explanation.walkthrough: L and R stand for left and right, so the L becomes R and the R becomes L.
explanation.definitionFit: A rowel is the spiked wheel of a spur, and as a verb it means to prick a horse with one.

clue.text: Local tack maker with welcoming word about Scottish inventor turning up

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for with
a greeting

indicators.note: in a down light, turning upwards means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: re means concerning
James Watt, the Scottish engineer who improved the steam engine

explanation.surface: A nearby saddler greets customers with a story about a famous Scot appearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' marks a dialect word, and tack here is horse gear, not a small nail.
explanation.definitionFit: A whittawer is a dialect word for a saddler or harness-maker; tack means saddles, bridles and similar gear.

clue.text: Old woman taking to heart the end for ancient king

indicators.note: the final letter is moved into the centre, a rearrangement of the word

parts.note: a crone is an old woman

explanation.surface: An elderly woman is deeply moved by the death of a monarch long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking to heart' sounds emotional, but it means the last letter goes to the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Creon was the ruler of Thebes in Greek myth, uncle of Antigone in Sophocles' tragedies.

clue.text: Lines I stuck in glue behind Private Eye cover's thickened part

indicators.note: coming after another part means placed later in the answer

parts.note: PTE is the military abbreviation for the rank of private
RY is the abbreviation for railway lines

indicators.note: something stuck in a substance is embedded within it

parts.note: gum is an adhesive
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone glues a satirical magazine's front page together.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye is a British satirical magazine; the surface wants it as one name, but the words split between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A pterygium is a wing-shaped growth of thickened conjunctiva, the membrane covering the eye.

clue.text: Concerned with syringes, rave about Torvill but …?

parts.note: the opposite of raving about someone is panning, savaging them in a review
the trailing dots ask for her skating partner, Christopher Dean

explanation.surface: A medical-sounding question about injections leads into gushing over an ice-skater.
explanation.walkthrough: Jayne Torvill and Christopher Dean were British Olympic ice-dance champions; praise one, criticise (pan) the other. Syringes here are the plural of syrinx, a set of panpipes.
explanation.definitionFit: Pandean means relating to the god Pan, and his pipes are called a syrinx, so it concerns those instruments.

clue.text: Just family, excluding north Siberian people

parts.note: fair and even-handed

indicators.note: to exclude something is to leave it out

parts.note: one's kin are one's relatives
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Only relatives are invited, leaving out the northern branch from Siberia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like 'only', but it means fair; the northern exclusion also suits a Siberian surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The Evenki are a Tungusic ethnic group of eastern Siberia, traditionally reindeer herders.

clue.text: Former groom's mate more amicable after cancelling yours truly and MC's half?

parts.note: a pal is a friend

indicators.note: cancelled items are struck out, so these letters are removed

parts.note: comparative of friendly
the writer referring to themselves
in Roman numerals MC is 1100, and half that is 550, written DL

explanation.surface: A bridegroom's best man becomes friendlier once the letter-writer and the master of ceremonies drop out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' and 'MC' paint a wedding, but the groom tends horses and MC is a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A palfrenier was a stable servant who looked after horses, an obsolete word for a groom.

clue.text: Pa thus taught in Scottish would be pink

indicators.note: the answer is what remains if a prefix is added to it and then removed again to reach the other phrase

parts.note: pink is a pale red
taken as written

explanation.surface: A father taught in a Scots accent would turn out a left-wing pink.
explanation.walkthrough: Put PA in front of the answer and you get 'pale red', which is pink.
explanation.definitionFit: Lere is an old Scots verb meaning to teach, and this is its past tense, learned or instructed.

clue.text: Example of minor third creature with off-putting smell

wordplay.note: the musical interval from the note A up to the note C spans a minor third

explanation.surface: A music lesson about a minor interval moves on to a smelly animal.
explanation.walkthrough: A minor third is a three-semitone interval, and A to C is a standard example of one.
explanation.definitionFit: An atoc is a skunk, an animal famous for spraying a foul defensive odour.

clue.text: Male, bachelor, following X channel to help clear the decks

definitions.text: channel to help clear the decks

indicators.note: coming after another part means placed later in the answer

parts.note: chi is the Greek letter written X
M is the abbreviation for male
B is the abbreviation for bachelor

explanation.surface: An unmarried man is following a channel on the platform formerly called Twitter.
explanation.walkthrough: X looks like the social media platform, but it is the Greek letter chi.
explanation.definitionFit: On a ship a chimb is a channel in the waterway along the deck edge, letting water drain off.

clue.text: British address shortly to be Indian man's address

indicators.note: cut short means losing the final letter

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
to hail someone is to call out to them

explanation.surface: A British home address is soon to become an Indian man's.
explanation.walkthrough: Both uses of 'address' suggest a home, but each is a form of greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Bhai means brother in Hindi and is used as a friendly way of speaking to a man in India.

clue.text: Dividing something banked in Gateshead, was a candidate to be dictatorial no more?

indicators.note: to divide is to split into two parts, which then sit either side of an insert

parts.note: a river has banks; the Tyne flows past Gateshead in north-east England
a candidate runs for office

explanation.surface: Splitting money deposited in a Gateshead bank, an election hopeful no longer wants to be a despot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banked' suggests money, but it means having banks, as a river does.
explanation.definitionFit: An obsolete verb meaning to act as a tyrant, so the question mark and 'no more' flag it as archaic.

clue.text: Kiwis' dance almost over: expect short perch for them

indicators.note: turned over means flipped end to end
nearly all means losing the final letter

parts.note: the haka is the Maori war dance performed by New Zealanders

indicators.note: cut short means losing the final letter

parts.note: to await is to expect

explanation.surface: New Zealanders' dance is nearly done, so expect a brief rest on a perch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Them' points back to the Kiwis, so the definition is a New Zealand fish; perch looks like a resting place.
explanation.definitionFit: The kahawai is a New Zealand sea fish, also called Australian salmon, related to perch-like fishes.

clue.text: Stimulus for casting eastern European's gripping return of curious detective constable

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came
to grip is to hold tight, so one piece holds another

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for eastern
E is the abbreviation for European
nosy means inquisitive
DC is the police abbreviation for detective constable

explanation.surface: A Continental film's casting is driven by an inquisitive police officer coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casting' sounds like choosing actors, but it means shedding skin, as insects do when moulting.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecdysone is the steroid hormone that triggers moulting in insects and crustaceans.

clue.text: Pointer to Mecca saving the man changing direction

indicators.note: turning to face the other way makes the letters run backwards

parts.note: bar means except, as does saving
a pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: A compass needle points towards Mecca while rescuing a man who keeps turning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saving' looks like rescue, but here it is the old preposition meaning except.
explanation.definitionFit: A mihrab is the niche in a mosque wall showing the qibla, the direction of Mecca for prayer.
